video_title: The Midterms Just Destroyed the AI Trade?
gist: Jordi Visser argues the 2026 midterm blue wave (including a Texas upset) adds political and regulatory friction to the AI buildout and accelerated a hedge-fund deleveraging that has erased over 60% of his agentic portfolio's YTD gains, but does not change compute demand. He frames the S&P 500 as '492 bonds and eight call options' facing post-2030 growth exhaustion and government targeting, while falling oil, peaking DRAM inflation and easing real yields turn liquidity into a tailwind for Bitcoin, which he sees near a textbook Elliott-wave correction low around its 200-day moving average.

themes.theme: Midterm blue wave vs. the AI buildout

insights.claim: Jordi Visser says the midterm sell-off was driven not by the Democrats winning (they were favored) but by the extent of the losses, especially the Texas governor upset after Abbott had been polling over 60%.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The surprise magnitude, not the direction, is what markets had to reprice.
insights.quote: it was the extent of the damage, it was Texas and the surprise because Abbott was over 60% going into it

insights.claim: Visser expects the midterm result to have little impact on 2027 AI construction because projects already under construction will be finished, but sees it making the next two years slower via heavier state regulation, especially a new Texas governor slowing data-center approvals.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Near-term capex is locked in; the risk is to the 2028 buildout timeline and permitting speed.
insights.quote: There's no way having a new governor in Texas won't slow down the process of getting it done.

insights.claim: Visser argues the election does not change the demand side of compute and that AI stocks, already significantly off their highs, had largely discounted the outcome.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: He treats the post-election drop as a positioning event rather than a fundamental demand break.
insights.quote: for me, I don't think this changes the demand side of compute. I don't think it changes the fact that the stocks had already discounted this.

insights.claim: According to Visser, the new Texas governor did not oppose data centers outright but wants financiers to pay for water and electricity impacts before projects go up, which raises costs and compresses margins for hyperscalers.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Expect higher local cost-of-doing-business levies on data centers rather than outright bans.
insights.quote: You're going to make sure electricity is taken care of. They're going to do that anyway, but it does come at the expense of margins.

insights.claim: Visser contends AI is broadly hated in the US and that wealth distribution, a central voter issue alongside affordability, is increasingly attached to AI, inviting more government intervention.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Political backlash against AI is a structural headwind for big public AI beneficiaries.
insights.quote: AI is hated in this country. It is absolutely hated and more and more that's become evident to me.

insights.claim: Visser believes the government will not allow a single AGI winner and is already more involved in AI than a year ago, citing Intel, OpenAI and Anthropic, because cyber risk has reached extreme levels.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Winner-take-all AI valuations face a regulatory ceiling.
insights.quote: if you don't think the government's going to get involved as this thing gets more dangerous, you're out of your mind.

insights.claim: Visser cites Microsoft offering buyouts to 27% of its employees as a warning sign that AI progress is moving faster than governments and large-headcount companies can handle.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: AI-driven labor displacement at mega-caps fuels the labor-vs-capital political backlash.
insights.quote: When Microsoft says they're going to get offer buyouts to 27% of their employees, how is that not like a major warning sign

insights.claim: Visser observes that newly elected officials are less centrist on both sides, and that starting from a 6% deficit neither heavy spending nor austerity will work, leaving the US on Lyn Alden's 'nothing stops this train' path.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Persistent deficits plus AI spending keep nominal growth going amid rising political extremism.
insights.quote: I think we're on this Lynn Alden nothing stops this train.

insights.claim: Anthony Pompliano notes a Raymond James chart showing Trump's approval rating tracking gas prices almost identically, and that young male voters swung back to blue, which he reads as voters chasing whoever promises to fix their problems rather than partisan loyalty.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Energy prices are a direct political lever; anti-incumbent swings are likely to continue.
insights.quote: Raymond James put out a chart that showed Trump's approval rating mapped onto the gas prices.

themes.theme: S&P 500 as 492 bonds and 8 call options

insights.claim: Visser endorses Marc Andreessen's framing that 492 S&P 500 companies are effectively bonds and eight (the Mag 7 plus SpaceX) are call options racing to dominate AI, and is writing a paper on it.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Most index constituents should be valued for income-like returns, not growth.
insights.quote: He said everything in the S&P 500 is basically 492 are bonds. Eight of them are call options which is exactly what I believe.

insights.claim: Visser predicts that by around 2030 growth for nearly all public companies with large workforces will be done because AI disrupts them, and they will deliver S&P-minus returns similar to Europe and emerging markets, which have done nothing since 2007.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Long-run passive US equity return assumptions may be too high for AI losers.
insights.quote: if you go to Europe, their stock market has done nothing since 2007. You go to emerging markets, it's done nothing.

insights.claim: Visser argues large public companies will be targeted by cyber attacks and government intervention, and that when government gets involved in public markets you cannot expect the same returns.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Size and AI-driven margins become liabilities, not moats.
insights.quote: If you're a big public company, you're targeted via cyber. You're targeted via government intervention.

insights.claim: Visser classifies AI infrastructure names like Nebius and CoreWeave as bonds rather than call options because he does not think they can grow 10x, though he expects infrastructure to deliver S&P-plus returns for only the next 2-3 years before efficiency gains erode it.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The AI infrastructure trade has a limited time window.
insights.quote: So if you think where Nebius is, where Corewave is, what how would you price them? They're effectively bonds.

insights.claim: Visser says the Mag 7 call options are being forced to spend enormous sums for a payoff that may not happen, citing Larry Page's reported willingness to bankrupt Google in the race to AGI.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Mega-cap capex converts former 'just own it' compounders into high-risk bets.
insights.quote: I'll bankrupt this company in the race to AGI

insights.claim: Visser notes the hyperscalers Meta, Amazon, Google and Microsoft have all had roughly 10% one-day falls in the last 12 months and have traded around flat for most of the year, unlike the low-volatility SaaS-and-ZIRP era of 2010-2019.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Holding mega-cap tech now requires trading, not buy-and-hold.
insights.quote: if you're investing in this stuff, you're becoming a trader whether you like it or not.

insights.claim: Visser contends there are no more moats, and that SpaceX, despite doing something different, may be the biggest government target in the world.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Even unique franchises face political risk that caps growth.
insights.quote: there are no more moes

insights.claim: Visser points to Dario Amodei building the most valuable company in the world while owning a small share, as evidence that founders of AI-native businesses face pressure against selling equity to public markets.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The best AI growth may stay private, starving public indexes of it.
insights.quote: So Dario has created the most valuable company in the world and how much does he own of it?

themes.theme: Hedge fund deleveraging and the AI trade drawdown

insights.claim: Visser states that peak hedge fund leverage has passed and the industry will never again be as levered in dollar terms.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A structural reduction in leveraged demand for crowded AI longs.
insights.quote: the peak of hedge fund leverage has passed. We will never ever ever again be as levered as we were in dollar terms overall.

insights.claim: Visser says his agentic AI portfolio has given back over 60% of its gains from the start of the year to the early-June peak, and every purchase he has made in recent months is underwater.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The AI trade drawdown is severe even for a committed bull who is still buying.
insights.quote: my agentic portfolio has given back over 60% of the gains that had happened from uh the beginning of the year till then

insights.claim: Visser reports rumors of two major hedge funds closing either entirely or their equity businesses, describing a Liberation Day-type panic selling day and a Roberto Duran 'no mas' moment for hedge funds.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Forced liquidations, not fundamentals, may be driving the latest leg down.
insights.quote: I think hedge funds reached the no MS moment

insights.claim: Visser attributes the October-to-early-November leg down in AI to a chain of shocks: CoreWeave debt, French debt, the Marvell acquisition, Intel, Google falling, followed by the midterms.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Cumulative idiosyncratic shocks broke levered holders' risk budgets.
insights.quote: I think Marll and Intel in particular last week had a huge impact on this next leg down that happened in AI.

insights.claim: Visser views Marvell's 100-plus-billion-dollar acquisition of a different part of the stack as unnecessary and risk-increasing, and it hurt his own position.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Large consolidation deals in a drawdown are being read as negative by holders.
insights.quote: this is not a good thing if it ends up happening just because I don't think it needs to be done.

insights.claim: Visser compares the current situation to LTCM: levered funds like Leopold Aschenbrenner's Situational Awareness may be in trouble not because Micron will miss numbers but because their leverage (e.g., $300-400 of positions per $100 of capital) leaves no time to stay in the trade.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Being right on fundamentals does not protect overlevered holders; watch for forced selling.
insights.quote: It's still like LTCM guys.

insights.claim: Visser notes the equal-weight S&P 500 hit an all-time high the day after the midterms even as AI names fell, meaning hedged AI longs had nowhere to hide as their shorts rose.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Market breadth rotation is squeezing long-AI/short-market books.
insights.quote: equal weight S&P made an all-time high the day after

insights.claim: Visser says the AI trade's 'June firework show' is over and from here it will be a grind, with no 3-month period free of risks like bubble fears, defaults or open-source price competition.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Lower expected returns and recurring volatility shocks for AI equities.
insights.quote: We're never again going to see what we saw in the first half for the Agentic Compute trade.

insights.claim: Visser argues that by slowing spending, the midterms eliminated near-term AI bubble risk because not enough debt or spending has yet occurred, pushing the buildout out and reducing capital needs that had pressured rates higher.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Slower capex is framed as bubble-deferring and rate-relieving, not as the end of the trade.
insights.quote: I think with the midterms, we've eliminated the the bubble risk, which sounds funny when the market's going down

insights.claim: Visser calls 2026 possibly one of the worst years in history for the S&P 500 relative to earnings: index gains are no longer double digits while earnings grow close to 30%, implying sharp multiple compression.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The market is pricing growing headwinds to equity growth despite strong earnings.
insights.quote: We're no longer up double digits, but earnings are growing close to 30%.

insights.claim: Visser says Micron trades at a P/E of about 3 and Nvidia is approaching a single-digit P/E, but he does not expect Micron to re-rate to a 10 P/E because he believes all multiples are coming down.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Low AI-hardware P/Es reflect structural de-rating, not an obvious value signal.
insights.quote: Do I think uh micron will ever get to a 10p? No.

insights.claim: Visser notes Apple is the only big company with real multiple expansion this year, at around a 40 P/E, because it has essentially zero AI capex and acts as a safe hedge; Apple, Berkshire and Eli Lilly are all at all-time highs.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Capital is rotating into AI-immune quality names as a hedge against AI capex risk.
insights.quote: They're actually immune to AI. They don't have an AI business.

insights.claim: Visser says Nvidia fell about 10% and Micron more than 10% on the recording day, with volatility inside the AI trade now far higher than Bitcoin's, which has stayed around 30 all year.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Bitcoin is now the lower-volatility asset relative to AI equities.
insights.quote: Bitcoin's volatility has stayed around 30 for basically the whole year.

insights.claim: Visser explains Qualcomm's 9% post-earnings drop as tied to autos and phones: car sales are weak on affordability and FSD has not rolled out, and memory bottlenecks have raised phone prices so Apple expects to sell fewer units.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Memory inflation is a second-order drag on non-data-center chip demand.
insights.quote: memory's been such a big bottleneck and it's made the prices go higher that Apple has said they're not going to sell as many as thought.

themes.theme: Liquidity turn: oil, DRAM, real yields

insights.claim: Visser explains that 10-year yields rose this year while inflation expectations fell since March, pushing real yields to high levels, which was a liquidity headwind for gold and Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Falling real yields would remove a key headwind for hard assets.
insights.quote: We saw bond yields go higher, but inflation expectations actually went down since March.

insights.claim: Visser notes 1-year and 2-year inflation expectations are now below where they started the year after Brent crude fell $20 in three days just before the election.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The oil drop is underappreciated and feeds directly into easier inflation and rates.
insights.quote: Brent crude was down $20 in 3 days and that happened right before the election

insights.claim: Visser says DRAM prices, a 2026 inflation contributor, have peaked in growth rate and are in negative year-over-year growth, with base effects intensifying by March since the biggest gains occurred September to March.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Memory-driven inflation fades into spring 2027.
insights.quote: DRM prices have already peaked uh not in terms of their actual price but in their growth rate.

insights.claim: Visser forecasts a sharply negative headline CPI print for November: pump gas has fallen from $4.40 to $4.10 and unleaded futures imply $3.75, roughly a 20% decline, and with tariffs rolling off and oil base effects after March he believes inflation fears have peaked.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A disinflation impulse supports lower rates and better liquidity for risk assets.
insights.quote: my whole estimate is that the inflation fears have peaked as well.

insights.claim: Visser cites Brad Gerstner's estimate that a slower AI buildout takes 50 basis points off GDP, which would lower growth and allow rates to come down.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Less AI capex could ease the rate pressure that hurt liquidity-sensitive assets.
insights.quote: Brad Gersner says this is 50 basis points off GDP

insights.claim: Visser flags that the Treasury's quarterly refunding announcement tweaked its language, as it did on August 4 before a buyback announcement two weeks later, signaling the government may act to keep long-end yields from hurting affordability.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Possible upsized Treasury buybacks could cap long-end yields.
insights.quote: they did this language change on August 4th as well. And then 2 weeks later on the 18th or 19th is when they actually made the buyback announcement

themes.theme: Iran, oil and the Vance-Trump split

insights.claim: Visser reads the pre-election oil drop as Iran signaling willingness to talk for the first time, with Khamenei giving the okay, after holding out until Trump's party lost, so Iran now negotiates from perceived strength.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: This oil decline may be more durable than earlier Trump-announced deal rallies.
insights.quote: This time, it was the Iranians that basically did this and the oil price dropped.

insights.claim: Visser argues Iran is losing leverage because the US blockade and bypass pipelines (expected in roughly 2-3 years) will erode its Strait of Hormuz chokehold, making now its best time to negotiate, and he sees less chance of a move higher in oil.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Skew on oil has shifted to the downside.
insights.quote: I think there's less chance than we thought of a move higher.

insights.claim: Pompliano highlights JD Vance saying the war was why Republicans lost, a divergence from Trump that Visser ties to Vance preparing for the 2028 election and to Republicans pushing to end the war.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Domestic political pressure raises the odds of a war resolution and lower oil.
insights.quote: JD said that he uh he believes the reason we lost is the war.

insights.claim: Visser notes that even when the Strait was truly shut, oil did not reach the levels people expected, suggesting something structurally different was happening in the oil market.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Supply-shock fears were overestimated, supporting a lower oil ceiling.
insights.quote: The price of oil did not go to the levels that people thought it would.

themes.theme: Bitcoin: correlation, flows and Elliott waves

insights.claim: Visser says Bitcoin is benefiting from an AI-driven world of no moats because it lacks the government-targeting hurdles of public stocks, and he expects tokenization and agentic commerce growth over the next two to three years to benefit it.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Bitcoin is positioned as a growth asset outside the government-targeted equity complex.
insights.quote: Bitcoin doesn't have the hurdles that stocks do.

insights.claim: Visser notes Bitcoin ETF outstanding shares hit new all-time highs despite the price being well off its highs, indicating wealth managers are still allocating, as banks now push to sell Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Sticky institutional demand underpins Bitcoin through the drawdown.
insights.quote: The outstanding shares for the Bitcoin ETF hit new all-time highs despite the fact that we are significantly off the all-time highs

insights.claim: Visser frames Bitcoin as correlated to the NASDAQ-over-S&P ratio (beta versus quality) and to gold, and expects it to rise with any AI bounce and gold rally, potentially with returns of roughly 1.5-3x the NASDAQ's.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Bitcoin is part gold, part NDX; positioning should reflect both drivers.
insights.quote: It's part gold at this point. It's part NDX.

insights.claim: Using Elliott wave analysis, Visser says Bitcoin completed a five-wave advance from the June lows to its recent peak and is now in a near-textbook three-wave correction toward its 200-day moving average around the 73-74 area (thousand), contingent on equities finding a low.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The 73-74k zone is his technical area for a Bitcoin low.
insights.quote: now we've seen a three-wave correction that is almost textbook getting now down to the 200 day moving average, which is right around the 7374 area.

insights.claim: Visser argues the liquidity headwinds for Bitcoin and gold began when the US and Israel went into Iran, raising real yields and Fed hike expectations, stalling dollar weakness, while the AI trade absorbed capital; he expects these headwinds to drop off.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Reversal of the Iran-driven liquidity squeeze is a catalyst for Bitcoin and gold.
insights.quote: I think the liquidity headwinds are going to drop off.

insights.claim: Visser says expectations swung from rate cuts at the start of the year to significant Fed rate hikes this year and into next year, which correlated with weakness in gold and Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Any unwind of hike expectations is a direct tailwind for hard assets.
insights.quote: we went from expectations of rate cuts at the beginning of the year to significant rate hikes not just this year but into next year.

insights.claim: Visser uses AI to extract approximate underlying data from chart images (Bloomberg, FT, Twitter), checks it against true data to correct errors, and merges charts with different timelines into one, which he says was not possible six months ago.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Multimodal models now enable fast cross-source chart synthesis for research.
insights.quote: It's now good enough to do this, which was not the case 6 months ago.

insights.claim: Pompliano built a Grok-based health coach bot connected to Garmin and Apple Health that tracks food via photos and follows its menu recommendations, illustrating growing willingness to let AI make personal decisions.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Consumer AI agents are moving into delegated daily decision-making.
